name: How to Dye Leather Armor in Minecraft
quickAnswer: In Java, combine leather armor with dyes in the crafting grid; in Bedrock, dip it in a water-filled cauldron dyed with any dye. Mix dyes for over 12 million color combos, and wash the armor in a cauldron to reset it.
steps: Craft leather armor from 24 leather for the full set (helmet, chestplate, leggings, boots).
Gather dyes: flowers, squid ink, cocoa beans, lapis and more - or craft mixed colors like purple, orange and lime.
Java: put the armor piece and any dyes anywhere in the crafting grid - every dye in the grid blends into the final color.
Bedrock: fill a cauldron with water, add dye to color the water, then dip the armor piece in.
Mix and match: re-dyeing an already dyed piece blends the old and new colors, giving millions of possible shades.
Wolf bonus: dye also colors the collar of a tamed wolf (since 1.4.2, same update).
Changed your mind? Use the dyed piece on a cauldron with plain water to wash the color out.
Show it off: dyed leather works on armor stands for base decoration and team uniforms.
materials: Cauldron + water (Bedrock dyeing, washing in both)
editionNote: This is one of the few real edition differences: Java dyes leather armor in the crafting grid, while Bedrock uses dyed cauldron water. Mixing colors and cauldron washing work in both, and wolf collar dyeing exists in both too.
versions: Dyeable leather armor and wolf collars were added in 1.4.2 (12w34a, Pretty Scary Update). Bedrock introduced its cauldron-dyeing method in Pocket v0.14.0, and the two systems have stayed different ever since.

faq.q: How many colors can leather armor be?
faq.a: Over 12 million. The game blends the RGB values of every dye applied, so each dye combination and each re-dye produces a unique shade - far beyond the 16 base dye colors.

faq.q: Can I dye iron or diamond armor?
faq.a: No - only leather armor (and leather horse armor) takes dye. Netherite, diamond, iron, gold and chainmail keep their fixed look, which is exactly why leather survives as the fashion tier.

faq.q: Does washing remove all the dye?
faq.a: Yes - using dyed leather armor on a cauldron with water resets it to the default brown. In Bedrock the same cauldron can hold dyed water, so mind you dip in the right one.

name: How to Tame an Axolotl in Minecraft
quickAnswer: Axolotls cannot be tamed like wolves, but they follow any player holding a bucket of tropical fish and fight for you in water - granting Regeneration and clearing Mining Fatigue when they help you kill a mob.
steps: Find axolotls in the dark waters of lush caves - they spawn in five colors: pink (lucy), brown (wild), gold, cyan, and the ultra-rare blue.
Catch them with a water bucket: using a bucket on an axolotl scoops it up, and bucketed axolotls never despawn.
Carry a bucket of tropical fish (not raw fish - it must be a live bucket catch) and nearby axolotls follow you.
Breed two axolotls by feeding each a bucket of tropical fish. The baby has a 1 in 1200 chance of being blue - the only way to get one.
Fight alongside them underwater: when an axolotl helps you kill a hostile mob, you get Regeneration I and any Mining Fatigue is removed - perfect for ocean monument raids.
Watch them play dead: a damaged axolotl drops still for 10 seconds, heals up, and enemies ignore it while it recovers.
Keep them wet: axolotls survive about 5 minutes out of water unless it is raining, so give your squad a pool at home.
materials: Buckets of tropical fish (to attract and breed)
editionNote: Behavior is the same in Java and Bedrock: bucket-catching, tropical fish following and breeding, combat Regeneration and play-dead all match. Blue axolotls are breeding-only (1 in 1200) in both editions since 1.17.1.
versions: Axolotls were added in 1.17 (20w51a, Caves and Cliffs part 1). Natural blue spawns existed for only a few months - 1.17.1 made blue breeding-exclusive, a nod to the roughly 1200 axolotls left in the wild in real life.

faq.q: Can you actually tame an axolotl?
faq.a: Not in the wolf-and-cat sense. They attach to whoever holds a bucket of tropical fish, they fight beside you, and bucketed ones are yours forever - but there is no collar, no sit command, and no ownership tag.

faq.q: Why are axolotls good for ocean monuments?
faq.a: Axolotls attack guardians, drowned, squid and fish, and when one helps you land a kill you get Regeneration I and your Mining Fatigue is wiped - the two things that make elder guardian fights miserable.

faq.q: How do I get a blue axolotl?
faq.a: Only by breeding: every baby axolotl has a 1 in 1200 (0.083%) chance of being blue. The odds honor the real axolotl, which survives in the wild only around Lake Xochimilco in Mexico City.

name: How to Find a Village in Minecraft
quickAnswer: Villages generate in plains, savanna, taiga, meadow, snowy plains and desert biomes (plus snowy taiga and sunflower plains in Bedrock). Explore those biomes on foot or with a cartographer explorer map, or use /locate structure with cheats.
steps: Target the right biomes: villages only generate in plains, savanna, taiga, meadow, snowy plains and desert - in Bedrock also snowy taiga and sunflower plains. Forests, jungles and mountains never have them.
Travel in a straight line through flat biomes: plains and deserts give the best sightlines, and village buildings are visible from far away.
Climb for height: a tall hill or a tower of blocks reveals villages several hundred blocks out, especially at night when their torches glow.
Use cheats if your world allows them: /locate structure minecraft:village_plains (or village_desert, village_savanna, village_taiga, village_snowy) gives exact coordinates.
Buy your way there: cartographer villagers sell explorer maps that lead to villages of other types - the map type depends on the villager's biome.
Rare find: 2% of villages generate as abandoned zombie villages - no doors, no torches, mossy cobblestone, and zombie villagers that never despawn.
Found one? Wall it off, light it up and ring the bell to start trading, breeding and iron golem farming.
materials: Food and blocks for a long trip
editionNote: Java and Bedrock share the six core village biomes, but Bedrock adds snowy taiga and sunflower plains. The /locate structure command works in both, and cartographer explorer maps exist in both editions.
versions: Villages have existed since Beta 1.8 (2011). The 1.14 Village and Pillage update rebuilt them per biome, 1.18 added meadow villages, and cartographer explorer maps arrived in 1.20.2 - making villages searchable without cheats for the first time.

faq.q: What is the fastest way to find a village?
faq.a: With cheats, /locate structure minecraft:village_plains wins instantly. Survival-only: pick a direction through plains or desert and travel - villages are spaced a few hundred blocks apart on average, so an elytra or horse cuts the search to minutes.

faq.q: Can villages spawn in any biome?
faq.a: No - only plains, savanna, taiga, meadow, snowy plains, desert, plus snowy taiga and sunflower plains in Bedrock. If a village center lands on a biome edge, the style is decided by the biome at the meeting point, defaulting to plains.

faq.q: What is a zombie village?
faq.a: A 2% generation chance replaces all villagers with zombie villagers and strips doors and torches. Nothing attacks you on sight there more than anywhere else - and you can cure the zombie villagers with weakness potions and golden apples to repopulate it.

keywords: how to find a village minecraft, minecraft village, locate village, village biomes, zombie village

name: How to Make a Map in Minecraft
quickAnswer: Surround a compass with 8 paper to craft an empty locator map, then use it to record the terrain around you. A cartography table lets you zoom it out (up to 4 times), clone it, and lock it with a glass pane.
steps: Craft paper from sugar cane - you need 8, so a cane farm pays off fast.
Craft a compass from 4 iron ingots around 1 redstone dust.
Place the compass in the center of the crafting table and surround it with 8 paper: one empty locator map.
Hold the map and press use to activate it - it records terrain in a 128-block radius (level 0/4).
Zoom out at a cartography table: map + paper enlarges the covered area, up to 4 times, ending at 2048x2048 blocks per map.
Clone maps with map + empty map at the cartography table - perfect for sharing with teammates.
Lock a finished map with map + glass pane so it never records again - and mark locations in Java by using the map on a placed banner.
Build a map wall: item frames with adjacent zoomed maps form a giant live map of your world.
materials: Cartography table (for zoom, clones and locks)
editionNote: Map crafting is identical in Java and Bedrock: compass + 8 paper for a locator map with a player marker. Zooming, cloning and glass-pane locking at the cartography table work in both; banner markers are Java-only.
versions: Maps were added in Beta 1.6 (2011), gained the compass-centered locator recipe in 1.4.2-era updates, and the cartography table arrived in 1.14 (Village and Pillage) with cheap zooming, cloning and locking.

faq.q: Why does my map not show where I am?
faq.a: A map only shows a white player marker if it is a locator map (crafted with a compass) and you are inside its recorded area. Zoomed-out maps show you as a smaller marker, and off the edge you only appear as a dot on the border.

faq.q: Map or coordinates?
faq.a: Coordinates (F3 in Java, world setting in Bedrock) are precise but ugly; maps are shareable, wall-mountable and mark banners and other players. Explorers carry both.

faq.q: How do I make a map wall?
faq.a: Zoom several maps to the same level covering adjacent areas, place item frames on a wall in the same arrangement, and insert each map. The wall updates live as you explore with a copy in hand.

keywords: how to make a map minecraft, minecraft map recipe, locator map, cartography table, map wall minecraft

name: How to Ride a Camel in Minecraft
quickAnswer: Camels are naturally tame - no taming needed. Find one in a desert village, put a saddle on it, and ride. They seat two players, dash up to 12 blocks, and stand so tall that zombies and vindicators cannot reach you.
steps: Find a camel: exactly one spawns in the center of every non-abandoned desert village at world generation.
Craft or find a saddle - camels are naturally tame, so no mounting ritual is needed.
Saddle up and ride: the camel seats two players, making it the only official two-seater mount.
Use the dash: hold the jump control to charge, release to launch up to 12 blocks forward and 1 block up. It recharges every 2.75 seconds.
Enjoy the height: while mounted, zombies, vindicators, hoglins, silverfish, endermites and sword-wielding piglins cannot reach you. Spiders, wolves and slimes still can.
Breed more with cactus: feed two camels cactus for a baby - but remember cactus blocks still hurt them on contact.
Camels sit down when idle: in Bedrock they stand as soon as you mount with a saddle; in Java they rise when you move forward.
editionNote: Riding, dashing and two-player seating are identical in Java and Bedrock. Small difference: Bedrock camels stand immediately when mounted with a saddle, while Java camels get up when you press forward. Dash distance and the mob-reach height advantage match in both.
versions: Camels were added in 1.20 (23w12a, Trails and Tales) as the first new mount in years. The 1.20.2 update refined their standing behavior, and the 26.x cycle even added their hostile desert cousin, the camel husk.

faq.q: Do you need to tame a camel?
faq.a: No - camels are naturally tame and always rideable. All you need is a saddle, which since 1.21.6 you can craft from 3 leather and 1 iron ingot instead of hunting loot chests.

faq.q: How far does a camel dash?
faq.a: A fully charged dash launches the camel up to 12 blocks forward and 1 block up, enough to clear rivers and ravine edges. The dash recharges every 2.75 seconds, shown on the experience bar.

faq.q: Camel or horse?
faq.a: Horse for speed and jump height; camel for safety and style - two seats, melee-proof height and a dash. For deserts, camels win because they outclass every local threat except spiders.

keywords: how to ride a camel minecraft, minecraft camel, camel dash, two player mount minecraft, desert village camel

name: How to Find a Ruined Portal in Minecraft
quickAnswer: Ruined portals generate in every biome in both the Overworld and the Nether - the only structure in two dimensions. Explore and watch for netherrack patches and obsidian frames; their chests hold gold gear, flint and steel, and obsidian.
steps: Understand the target: ruined portals spawn in every biome of the Overworld AND the Nether, on the surface, underground or underwater. 5% generate as giant portals.
Look for the signs: a patch of netherrack (including stalactite-like shapes) with an obsidian frame, often with crying obsidian mixed in.
While caving, watch for air pockets with netherrack - underground ruined portals generate surrounded by air.
Ocean travel works too: drowned-infested netherrack mounds on the seabed are usually underwater portals.
Loot the chest: gold ingots and nuggets, golden tools and armor, flint and steel, fire charges, obsidian, golden apples, bells - and since 1.21.5, sometimes a lodestone.
Use it: the obsidian frame plus a flint and steel is often enough obsidian to light your first Nether portal without a diamond pickaxe.
Nether-side portals matter too: a ruined portal near your Nether spawn is free obsidian and a landmark.
materials: Flint and steel (or from the chest)
editionNote: Ruined portals generate identically in Java and Bedrock: all biomes in both dimensions, 5% giant variants, the same loot table family including lodestones since 1.21.5. Both editions let you complete the frame and light it.
versions: Ruined portals were added in 1.16 (20w16a, the Nether Update), which is why their loot leans golden. Lodestones joined their chest loot in 1.21.5, making ruined portals a rare source of that wayfinding block.

faq.q: What is inside a ruined portal chest?
faq.a: Gold gear, gold ingots and nuggets, flint and steel, fire charges, obsidian, golden apples, enchanted golden tools, bells and clocks - thematically the leftovers of whoever broke the portal. Since 1.21.5, lodestones can appear too.

faq.q: Can I repair a ruined portal?
faq.a: Yes - that is their secret purpose. Replace the crying obsidian (it does not light) with regular obsidian, fill the gaps, and ignite with flint and steel from the chest. Many speedrunners find their first portal this way.

faq.q: Why is there crying obsidian in the frame?
faq.a: Crying obsidian is decorative and cannot form a working portal - you must mine it out (diamond or netherite pickaxe) and swap in normal obsidian. Save the crying obsidian for respawn anchors.

Craft a bowl from 3 planks.
Place 6 beetroots in the top two rows of the crafting table with the bowl at the bottom.
Eat for 6 hunger and 7.2 saturation - exactly mushroom-stew-tier food.

Leftover beetroot? Dye things red, breed pigs, or trade it to farmer villagers.

faq.q: Is beetroot soup worth making?
faq.a: Stat-wise it matches mushroom stew (6 hunger, 7.2 saturation), so it is fine - but 6 beetroots per bowl makes it expensive unless you run a beetroot farm. Most players grow beetroot for red dye and pig breeding instead.

faq.q: Where do I find beetroot seeds?
faq.a: Village farms are the fastest source - just harvest the beetroot already growing there. Seeds also show up in dungeon, mineshaft, woodland mansion and village chests, and end city chests can hold beetroot too.

faq.q: Beetroot soup or mushroom stew?
faq.a: Same hunger and saturation, same bowl back, same no-stacking. Mushroom stew wins on ingredient effort (2 mushrooms vs 6 beetroots), beetroot soup wins if your base is already a beetroot empire.

name: How to Get a Trident in Minecraft
quickAnswer: Tridents cannot be crafted. Kill drowned that spawn holding one: 6.25% of natural drowned carry a trident, and it drops with 8.5% chance in Java or 25% in Bedrock. Trial chamber vaults can also rarely give one.

Hunt the ones holding a trident: 6.25% of naturally spawned drowned have one.
Kill it with Looting III if you can: base drop chance is 8.5% in Java and 25% in Bedrock, and Looting raises it.
Farm it: an ocean ruin or river farm that spawns natural drowned produces tridents over time - converted-zombie farms do not.
Alternative: trial chamber vaults can rarely contain tridents.
Enchant it: Loyalty returns the thrown trident, Riptide launches you in water or rain, Channeling summons lightning in thunderstorms, Impaling adds damage.

editionNote: The big edition gap is drop rate: 8.5% in Java versus 25% in Bedrock per trident-wielding drowned killed by a player or tamed wolf. Riptide and Channeling work in both, and neither edition lets you craft a trident.
versions: Tridents were added in 1.13 (the Update Aquatic) alongside drowned. Trial chambers (1.21) added vaults as a second rare source, ending eight years of drowned-only farming.

faq.q: Can you craft a trident?
faq.a: No - the trident is famously uncraftable. Your sources are drowned that spawn holding one and, since 1.21, trial chamber vaults. That rarity is why Mending matters so much on a good one.

faq.q: Why does my drowned farm never drop tridents?
faq.a: If your farm converts zombies into drowned, that is the problem: converted drowned never spawn with tridents. Only naturally spawned drowned (6.25% chance) carry them - farms must generate natural spawns.

faq.q: Riptide or Loyalty?
faq.a: They are mutually exclusive, so most players carry two tridents: Loyalty for combat (it returns after every throw) and Riptide for travel, launching you through water and rain. Channeling pairs with Loyalty for thunderstorm lightning.

Touch water or rain within range and you get Conduit Power: water breathing, underwater night vision and faster underwater mining.

faq.q: What does Conduit Power actually do?

faq.q: How many prismarine blocks do I need?
faq.a: 16 blocks activate the conduit at 32 blocks of range, and every 7 additional blocks add 16 more range, up to 42 blocks for the full 96-block sphere. Prismarine, bricks, dark prismarine and sea lanterns all count.

faq.q: Is a conduit worth the 8 nautilus shells?
faq.a: For any underwater project, yes - it replaces water-breathing potions forever, lights the depths, speeds mining and even zaps guardians. Farm shells from drowned and wandering traders, and grab the heart from buried treasure.

name: How to Get a Heart of the Sea in Minecraft

faq.q: Is the heart of the sea in every buried treasure?

name: How to Find a Shipwreck in Minecraft
quickAnswer: Shipwrecks generate in oceans and on beaches, sometimes even inland or in ice. Sail the ocean watching for wooden masts, and loot up to 3 chests - the map chest in the stern always holds a buried treasure map.

Check the shallows too: many wrecks sit half-buried on beaches, visible from land.
Loot smart: wrecks hold up to 3 chests depending on intact sections - supply chest in the bow, treasure chest in the upper stern, map chest in the lower stern.

Cheat option: /locate structure minecraft:shipwreck gives exact coordinates.

versions: Shipwrecks were added in 1.13 (18w11a, the Update Aquatic) and made somewhat rarer in 1.16. They remain the only reliable source of buried treasure maps in the game.

faq.q: How many chests are in a shipwreck?

faq.q: Can shipwrecks spawn on land?
faq.a: Yes - wrecks generate on beaches and occasionally fully inland or frozen into icebergs, a leftover of Aquatic-era generation. Land wrecks are the easiest loot in the ocean update: no diving, no drowned ambush.

faq.q: Why do shipwrecks matter?
faq.a: Their map chests guarantee a buried treasure map, and buried treasure is the only source of hearts of the sea - the conduit ingredient. Every serious ocean playthrough starts with a wreck.

name: How to Find an Ocean Monument in Minecraft
quickAnswer: Ocean monuments generate only in deep ocean biomes and their variants. Sail the deep ocean looking for prismarine towers, buy an ocean explorer map from a cartographer, or use /locate structure minecraft:monument.
steps: Target deep ocean biomes - monuments never generate in shallow seas, rivers or warm shallows.
Sail with a boat and night vision or water breathing potions; monument lanterns are visible from the surface at night.
Buy your way: apprentice cartographers sell ocean explorer maps for 13 emeralds and a compass, leading straight to a monument.
Cheat option: /locate structure minecraft:monument gives exact coordinates.

name: How to Make a Compass in Minecraft

steps: Mine or smelt 4 iron ingots and 1 redstone dust.
Place the redstone in the center of the crafting table with an iron ingot on each side (top, bottom, left, right).

Upgrade 1 - lodestone compass: use a compass on a lodestone and it points to that block instead, across any distance. Works in the Nether and End too, where normal compasses just spin.

faq.a: Normal compasses only work in the Overworld - in the Nether and End they spin aimlessly. The fix is a lodestone compass: place a lodestone in the dimension you are in and bind the compass to it.

name: How to Make a Nether Portal
quickAnswer: Build a vertical rectangular frame of obsidian blocks - 4x5 minimum, 23x23 maximum, and the corners are optional - then light the inside with flint and steel or a fire charge. Build the frame. Place obsidian as a vertical rectangle at least 4 wide and 5 tall. Skip the four corners to save obsidian: two vertical sides of 3 blocks plus top and bottom rows of 2 blocks is just 10 obsidian. Maximum size is 23x23.
Light it. Use flint and steel or a fire charge on the inside of the frame. A ghast fireball or lava catching nearby wood alight also works. The frame fills with the purple portal.
Walk through. Stand inside the portal for a few seconds to travel to the Nether. One block travelled in the Nether equals eight in the Overworld, so long journeys are far shorter through portals.
Prepare before entering. Take iron armor or better, food, blocks and a gold item to keep piglins neutral. Never dig straight down in the Nether and mark your portal's coordinates.

faq.a: 10 with the corners skipped, 14 for the full 4x5 frame.

faq.q: Why won't my portal light?
faq.a: Check the frame is complete, vertical and inside the size limits, that you aren't in the End, and that no crying obsidian is in the frame.

faq.q: What is the 8-to-1 rule?
faq.a: Each block in the Nether equals 8 blocks in the Overworld. Two portals 100 blocks apart in the Nether link to Overworld points 800 blocks apart.

name: How to Use Redstone
quickAnswer: Redstone dust carries power up to 15 blocks from a source (lever, button, pressure plate, redstone torch) to a mechanism (door, piston, lamp, dispenser). Signal strength drops 1 per block, so use repeaters to extend it and torches to invert it. Master these four parts - source, dust, repeater, torch - and you can build almost anything.
steps: Learn the four core parts. Power sources (levers, buttons, pressure plates, redstone torches and blocks), redstone dust to carry the signal, repeaters to extend and delay it, and torches to invert it. Everything else is combinations of these.

Place dust to make wire. Redstone dust on the ground forms a line that powers the block it points into and the block beneath it. It carries power up to 15 blocks - the brightness shows the strength, fading as it travels.

Extend with repeaters. A repeater refreshes a weak signal back to full strength, adds a 0.1-0.4 second delay (right-click to change), and only lets power flow one way - perfect for long lines and timing circuits.

Invert with torches. A redstone torch on the side of a block turns off when that block is powered and on when it isn't. This NOT-gate is how you make doors that open when a plate is stepped off, or lights that come on at night with a daylight sensor.

Power mechanisms. Run your wire into pistons (push blocks), dispensers (shoot items), droppers, note blocks, lamps, doors and trapdoors. A powered block can also activate any mechanism touching it - that's how hidden wiring works.
editionNote: Core mechanics are the same in Java and Bedrock, but Java has quasi-connectivity (pistons and droppers can be powered from one block above like doors) while Bedrock doesn't - so some Java tutorials break on Bedrock. Repeater locking works in both editions.
versions: Redstone arrived in Alpha 1.0.1 (2010) as 'red ore' and powered the first doors. Repeaters came in Beta 1.3, comparators in 1.5, and observers in 1.11 - the four building blocks have been stable ever since.

faq.q: Why does my redstone stop after 15 blocks?
faq.a: That's the signal limit - dust carries power 15 blocks from the source. Place a repeater before it dies to refresh it to full strength and go another 15.

faq.q: What does a comparator do?
faq.a: It reads container fullness (chests, hoppers, furnaces), compares or subtracts two signals, and keeps the signal strength instead of refreshing it. The classic uses: item detectors, hopper clocks and password circuits.

faq.q: Why does my Java piston fire when it shouldn't?

name: How to Make a Piston Door
quickAnswer: The classic 2x2 flush piston door uses 4 sticky pistons (two per side, facing inward) that pull 2 wall blocks aside when you step on pressure plates. Wire each pair with redstone and a torch tower so one input fires all four pistons, and the wall melts away in front of you.
steps: Gather the parts. 4 sticky pistons (piston + slimeball each), redstone dust, 2 redstone torches, 4 pressure plates (or buttons), and the wall blocks you want the door to blend into.
Place the pistons. Dig a 2-wide, 2-tall doorway in your wall. On each side, place 2 sticky pistons one block behind the doorway, facing inward - one at floor level, one above it.
Set the door blocks. Put your wall blocks directly in front of each piston head, filling the 2x2 opening. When the pistons retract, they pull these blocks back and the doorway opens.

Wire one side. Run dust from each piston down to a central point and up a torch tower: a redstone torch under the block holding the lower piston's circuit inverts the signal so the door stays closed by default.

Add the pressure plates. Place 2 plates inside and 2 outside the door and connect them to the torch tower input. Step on any plate - power kills the torch, all four pistons retract together, and the door opens. Walk through and it closes behind you.
editionNote: The classic 2x2 design works identically in Java and Bedrock. Bigger doors (3x3, 4x4, seamless) rely on Java-only behaviors like quasi-connectivity and piston spitting, so follow an edition-specific tutorial for those.
versions: Pistons were added in Beta 1.7 (2011) and sticky pistons in Beta 1.8 - the 2x2 door design appeared within days and is still the most-built redstone contraption in the game.

faq.q: Why does only one side of my door open?
faq.a: The two sides aren't wired to the same input. Run both piston pairs to the single torch tower so one pressure plate signal reaches all four pistons at once.

faq.q: The door opens but doesn't close. What happened?
faq.a: A missing torch inversion: the pistons should be powered OFF by the torch when nobody is on the plate. Check the torch tower - a broken or misplaced torch leaves the door stuck open.

faq.q: Can I hide it completely?
faq.a: Yes - use the same block as your wall for the door blocks, bury the wiring under the floor, and cover the plates with carpet... no wait, plates can't be covered. Hide them in the doorway itself; that's the standard trade-off.

name: How to Make a Redstone Clock
quickAnswer: The easiest redstone clock is a repeater loop: 2 or more repeaters wired in a circle with a lever to start it, pulsing forever. For longer periods use a hopper clock - two hoppers passing items between them with comparators reading them - or an observer clock that pulses twice per second. Clocks power farms, doors and light shows.
steps: Build a repeater clock (fast). Place 2 repeaters in a loop facing each other with dust between them, pulse it with a lever flick, and it cycles forever. Add more repeaters (up to 0.4s delay each) to slow the pulse.
Build an observer clock (simplest). Face two observers into each other - each watches the other change and fires back, creating a compact 2-pulses-per-second clock with zero wiring.

Build a hopper clock (slow and precise). Place 2 hoppers facing into each other, put 1-64 items inside, and read one with a comparator. The items shuttle back and forth at 2.5 items per second; one item gives about a 0.8-second cycle, a full stack about 51 seconds.
Kill the flicker. Torch clocks (a torch with dust looping back into its own block) pulse fast but burn out and restart randomly - use repeaters or observers instead for anything important.
Hook it to your machine. Run the clock output into pistons (item elevators), dispensers (auto-farms), droppers, or note blocks. Add a lever in the line to switch the whole machine on and off.
editionNote: Repeater and hopper clocks behave the same in Java and Bedrock. Observer clocks differ slightly in timing between editions, and comparator repeater-lock tricks are Java-only. Burned-out torch clocks recover on their own in both.
versions: Hopper clocks became possible when hoppers and comparators arrived in 1.5 (the Redstone Update, 2013), and observer clocks arrived with observers in 1.11. The repeater loop is the oldest clock design, from Beta 1.3.

faq.q: Which clock should I use?
faq.a: Observer pair for fast pulsing (farms, dispensers), hopper clock for slow cycles (mob farm flushing, item sorters), repeater loop for anything in between with fine delay control.

faq.q: Why did my repeater clock stop?
faq.a: If the loop ever loses its pulse (chunk unload, lever timing), it stays dead. Build in a starter: a lever or button that re-injects a pulse, or use a self-starting design with a torch.

faq.q: Do clocks cause lag?
faq.a: Fast clocks with many pistons or hoppers can. Use the slowest clock that does the job, and turn machines off with a lever when you're not using them.

name: How to Use a Redstone Repeater in Minecraft
quickAnswer: A redstone repeater does four jobs: it refreshes a fading signal back to full strength 15, works as a one-way diode (signals only pass from back to front), adds an adjustable delay of 0.1 to 0.4 seconds, and locks its output state when another repeater or comparator powers its side. Right-click it to cycle through the four delay settings.
steps: Craft or loot one. A repeater takes 3 stone (smelted cobblestone), 2 redstone torches and 1 redstone dust - or grab the two that generate naturally in every jungle temple.
Place it facing the right way. The arrow on top points from input to output. A repeater only accepts a signal at its back and only outputs from its front, so a backwards repeater does nothing.
Extend a dying signal. Dust fades by 1 strength per block and dies at 15. Put a repeater just before that point and it re-emits at full 15, buying another 15 blocks. Chain them for long wires.

Set the delay. Right-click (use) the repeater to move the little torches apart: the four settings are 1, 2, 3 and 4 redstone ticks (0.1, 0.2, 0.3 and 0.4 seconds). Every repeater adds at least 0.1s, so account for it in timed circuits.

Use it as a diode. Because signals only travel one way through a repeater, placing one between two circuit sections stops them back-feeding into each other - the classic fix when a piston door fires itself.

Lock it for memory cells. Power the side of a repeater with another repeater or a comparator pointing into it and it freezes in its current on or off state until the side signal stops. Two side-locked repeaters in a loop make a 1-bit memory cell.
materials: Redstone repeater (3 stone + 2 redstone torches + 1 redstone dust)
Redstone dust and a lever for testing
Optional: a comparator or second repeater to try locking
editionNote: Works the same in Java and Bedrock, including side-locking. The one difference to watch: Java pulses shorter than the set delay get stretched to match it, which makes some 1-tick Java circuits behave differently from Bedrock builds.
versions: Repeaters have been in the game since Java Beta 1.3 (February 2011), and two generate in every jungle temple since 1.3.1. The four delay settings and side-locking have been stable ever since.

faq.q: How many repeaters do I need for a long wire?
faq.a: One for every 15 blocks of dust. Each repeater resets the signal to full strength 15, so a 100-block run needs about 6-7 repeaters - each adding at least 0.1 seconds of delay.

faq.q: Why is my repeater not powering the next block?
faq.a: It is probably facing backwards - the arrow must point away from the input. Also check that you are powering its back, not its side: a side signal locks the repeater instead of passing through.

faq.q: What does locking a repeater do?
faq.a: A side-powered repeater freezes its output: if it was on, it stays on even when the back input turns off, and vice versa, until the side signal releases it. That is the basis of memory cells and hidden-input locks.

name: How to Use a Redstone Comparator in Minecraft
quickAnswer: A redstone comparator has two modes. In compare mode (default) it passes its back input through only if that signal is at least as strong as any side input. Click the front torch to switch to subtract mode, which outputs the back signal minus the strongest side signal. Placed against a container, it instead reads how full the container is.
steps: Craft it. A comparator takes 3 stone, 3 redstone torches and 1 nether quartz - the quartz means one Nether trip first.

Learn the layout. The two short prongs face the input (back), the single torch is the output (front), and the two bare sides accept comparison signals. Unlike a repeater, a comparator keeps the signal strength as-is instead of refreshing it to 15.

Compare mode (front torch off, the default): the output equals the back input only if the back is stronger than or equal to both side inputs; otherwise the output is off. Use it to require two conditions at once.

Subtract mode (click the comparator so the front torch lights up): output = back signal minus the strongest side signal. Feed a 15-strength input and a 3-strength side and you get 12 out - the basis of analog counters.

Read containers. Against a chest, hopper, furnace, barrel, shulker box, cake, item frame, lectern, jukebox or command block, the comparator ignores signals and outputs 0-15 based on fullness or state. A full double chest gives 15; each cake slice left changes the level.

Build an item filter. Put exact filler stacks in a hopper so the comparator reads strength 2-3, run that through a torch and back into the hopper below - the classic design only unlocks when enough of the target item arrives. This is the heart of every storage system.
Mind the delay. A comparator always adds 1 game tick (0.05s) of delay, half a repeater tick, which matters in fast clocks.
materials: Redstone comparator (3 stone + 3 redstone torches + 1 nether quartz)
Chest or hopper to practice container reading
Redstone dust and a lamp to see the output
editionNote: Compare, subtract and container reading work the same in Java and Bedrock. One Java quirk: comparators can read some block states (like a cake or item frame rotation) through a solid block, which Bedrock does not always replicate - test filters on your edition.
versions: Comparators arrived in Java 1.5, the Redstone Update (January 2013), and container measuring was added in the same snapshot cycle. The recipe and both modes have been unchanged since.

faq.q: What is the difference between a repeater and a comparator?
faq.a: A repeater refreshes the signal to full 15 and only passes one way. A comparator keeps the exact strength, can subtract signals, and reads container fullness - but it does not boost a fading signal.

faq.q: How do I make a comparator read a chest?
faq.a: Place it with its back against the chest (or a block in front of the chest) and dust on the output. The signal strength scales with fullness: roughly empty = 0, one stack in a chest = 1, completely full = 15.

faq.q: Why does my item filter overflow or jam?
faq.a: The filler items in the filter hopper must be ones that stack to 64 and cannot match the sorted item in the wrong slots. If the comparator reads a strength above 3 the filter opens for everything - keep exactly the classic 41-target-item plus 1-1-1-1 filler layout.

name: How to Use an Observer in Minecraft
quickAnswer: An observer watches the block directly in front of its face. When that block changes - grows, is placed, broken or changes state - the red dot on the back fires a 1-redstone-tick pulse at full power 15. That single pulse powers farms, traps, flying machines and the fastest compact clocks in the game.
steps: Craft it. An observer takes 6 cobblestone, 2 redstone dust and 1 nether quartz, so it needs one Nether trip.

Place it facing the right way. The face with the two "eyes" watches the block in front of it; the red dot on the opposite side is the output. The face points away from you when you place it, so stand on the output side.
Wire the output. The dot side emits a pulse of strength 15 lasting 1 redstone tick (2 game ticks) - enough to fire a piston, dispenser or note block, or to feed dust, a repeater or a comparator.
Detect crop growth. Point the face at the top of sugar cane, bamboo, kelp or a cactus: when it grows one block, the observer fires once - the trigger behind most automatic farms.
Make a fast clock. Two observers facing each other detect each other pulsing and loop forever - the most compact fast clock in the game. Break and replace one to stop it.

Build a flying machine. An observer moved by a piston emits a pulse as it arrives, so two observers plus two slime blocks and pistons push each other along in a line. That is the engine of every flying machine.
materials: Observer (6 cobblestone + 2 redstone dust + 1 nether quartz)
Pistons and slime blocks for flying machines
Something to watch: crops, a furnace, a door
editionNote: Java and Bedrock observers detect different changes. Java watches for block-state "shape updates" (very predictable); Bedrock acts as a general block-update detector and fires on some changes Java ignores - and vice versa. Farm designs are rarely cross-edition compatible, so build one made for your edition.
versions: The observer debuted in Pocket Edition 0.15.0 (June 2016) as the first official BUD block, then came to Java in 1.11, the Exploration Update (November 2016). Its pulse has been 1 redstone tick at strength 15 ever since.

faq.q: Why does my observer fire randomly?
faq.a: It detects more than growth: block placement, breaking, water flowing in, even a chest being opened nearby on Bedrock. Check what block its face actually points at - one block off and it watches the wrong thing.

faq.q: Observer vs comparator for farms - which one?
faq.a: Use an observer to catch a change the moment it happens (cane grew, melon spawned). Use a comparator to measure a level (how full a chest is). Most automatic farms use observers as the trigger and comparators in the storage system.

faq.q: How do I stop an observer clock?
faq.a: Two facing observers pulse each other forever. Power one of their outputs into a piston that pushes a solid block between them, or just break one observer and place it back when you want the clock to run again.

name: How to Make a Hopper in Minecraft
quickAnswer: Craft a hopper with 5 iron ingots and a chest in a V shape: iron in the top corners and middle sides, the chest in the center, and one iron below it. A hopper collects dropped items above it and moves items between containers at 2.5 items per second - it is the pipe that connects every automatic farm.
steps: Smelt 5 iron ingots and craft a chest (8 planks). The recipe needs a crafting table.
Open the table and place iron in the top-left and top-right slots, iron in the middle-left and middle-right, the chest in the center, and the last iron below the chest. Take the hopper.

Place it pointing where items should go. Crouch (sneak) and right-click the container you want it to feed - the hopper attaches with its nozzle pointing into that container. Without sneaking you just open the container.
Feed it from above. A hopper pulls items out of a container sitting directly on top of it, and sucks up item entities that land on the block space above it.
Chain hoppers into pipes. Hoppers push into the hopper they point at, and hoppers below also pull, so you can run horizontal or vertical item lines across your base.
Lock it with redstone when needed. A powered hopper stops pushing and pulling (items already inside stay put). Levers, torches and comparators all work - this is how sorters and farms control flow.
Expect 2.5 items per second. After each transfer a hopper waits 8 game ticks (0.4s), so a single hopper line moves about a stack every 26 seconds. Use parallel lines or minecart hoppers for bulk.
materials: 5 iron ingots (smelted from iron ore or raw iron)
editionNote: Hoppers work the same in Java and Bedrock for everyday use. Behind the scenes they differ in performance details (Java prefers a composter or container on top of long hopper lines, Bedrock prefers air) and in a few pulling edge cases, but every normal farm works on both.
versions: Hoppers were added in Java 1.5, the Redstone Update (January 2013), with the same iron-and-chest recipe they still use today. They came to Pocket Edition in 0.14.0.

faq.q: Why is my hopper not taking items?
faq.a: Two common causes: it is powered by redstone (a powered hopper locks and stops moving items - remove the lever or torch), or it is pointing into a full container. Also check the item has somewhere to go: a hopper with a full destination stops pulling.

faq.q: How do I make a hopper point into a chest?
faq.a: Crouch and right-click the side of the chest with the hopper in hand. The nozzle visibly bends toward the block you clicked. A hopper placed on top of a chest points down into it automatically.

faq.q: Hopper or water stream for moving items?
faq.a: Water streams are far faster and cheaper for long distances and item collection; hoppers are for precise delivery, container-to-container transfer and redstone control. Most big farms use water to gather and a short hopper line to sort and store.

name: How to Make an Item Sorter in Minecraft
quickAnswer: An item sorter uses a hopper filled with exactly 41 of the target item plus 4 single filler items, a comparator reading that hopper, and a redstone torch that locks a second hopper below. When extra target items raise the signal from 2 to 3, the torch unlocks and the sorter pulls the extras into a chest - everything else flows past to the next module.
steps: Learn the one-line idea. A comparator reads how full the filter hopper is. The filter is tuned so only the target item can raise the signal, and the raised signal briefly unlocks a hopper that drains the overflow into a chest.

Build the base module. Run a line of hoppers into a row of chests. Behind each, place a second hopper (the filter) facing into a solid block, with a comparator reading it, dust, and a redstone torch that locks the hopper below the filter.

Load the filter correctly. Put 41 of the item you want to sort in the first slot, then ONE filler item in each of the other four slots. Fillers must stack to 64 and must never appear in your storage input - named or junk items like sticks work.

Understand the signal. With 41+1+1+1+1 the comparator outputs strength 2. When more target items arrive the stack grows, the output hits 3, the torch turns off and the lower hopper unlocks just long enough to drain the extras, then relocks. Other items cannot raise the signal, so they slide past.

Repeat the module per item. Tile the same build once per item type along your input line, each feeding its own chest. Leave one-hopper gaps or use the standard tileable layout so neighboring redstone does not cross-talk.

Protect against overflow. If a chest fills completely, its filter backs up and can break the module next door. Give every sorted item enough chest space, or add an overflow chest at the end of the line for unsorted items.

Test before trusting it. Throw a stack of the target item and a stack of junk into the input. The target lands in its chest and the junk travels to the unsorted bin - then it is safe to connect your farm output.
materials: Per item: 2 hoppers, 1 comparator, 1 redstone torch, 1 chest
Redstone dust and solid building blocks
41 of each item to sort + 4 filler items per module
Input line: hoppers or a water stream
editionNote: The classic filter works in Java and Bedrock. In Java, comparators can read the filter hopper through a solid block, which the common compact layouts rely on; Bedrock versions of the same design may need the comparator directly against the hopper. Build a design made for your edition.
versions: Item sorters have been possible since comparators arrived in Java 1.5 (2013), and the 41-plus-filler filter design has been the community standard ever since - it still works unchanged in the latest versions.

faq.q: Why did my sorter break and mix items?
faq.a: Almost always an overflow: the chest filled, the filter hopper backed up past 41 items, and the module started passing the target item downstream. Empty the chest, refill the filter to exactly 41+1+1+1+1, and give high-volume items more storage.

faq.q: Can I sort unstackable items like tools or armor?
faq.a: Not with the classic filter - it depends on stack counting. Unstackables need dedicated designs (usually with a hopper trying to match the item) or simply a manual chest. Most players send everything unstackable to the unsorted bin.

faq.q: How many items can one sorter handle?
faq.a: A single filter hopper moves 2.5 items per second, so one module handles most farms. For very fast farms (raid, gold), split the input across several parallel sorters or pre-sort with water streams into multiple lines.

name: How to Make a Flying Machine in Minecraft
quickAnswer: A flying machine is a self-moving engine: two observers facing into each other, each backed by a sticky piston, linked by slime blocks. An observer moved by a piston fires a pulse, which powers the other piston, which moves the machine and re-triggers the observers - so the whole build crawls forward forever. It farms sugar cane, clears land and moves bridges with zero fuel.
steps: Gather the parts. The minimal one-way engine needs 2 observers, 2 sticky pistons and 3-6 slime blocks. Slime blocks come from 9 slimeballs each, so hunt slimes in swamps at night or in slime chunks below Y 40.

Understand the loop. A piston that moves an observer makes that observer emit a pulse as it lands. Aim that pulse at the other piston and it pushes the whole assembly one block, which moves the first observer, which pulses again. Motion and triggering feed each other.

Build the classic engine. Place a sticky piston facing forward. Attach an observer behind it with the dot toward the piston. Mirror the same assembly facing the other way and connect both with slime blocks, keeping the total under the 12-block push limit.

Stay under 12 blocks. A piston can only move 12 blocks at once, and every slime block, observer and piston counts. If the engine refuses to move, count the connected blocks - one extra block welded on by accident is the usual cause.

Launch it. Place or remove a block to update one observer, or give one piston a quick pulse. The machine starts crawling. To stop it, place an immovable block (obsidian, furnace, a leaf block works on some designs) in its path.

Keep slime and honey apart. Slime blocks and honey blocks never stick to each other - that is a feature: two engine halves built from different sticky blocks can slide past each other without welding together. Use honey where you want a moving floor that does not grab the slime parts.

Add a job. Slime blocks launch entities they push, so riders and TNT go along for the ride. Attach note blocks or extra observers as outputs and the same engine becomes a sugar cane harvester, a tunnel bore or a moving bridge.
materials: 2 observers (6 cobblestone + 2 redstone dust + 1 quartz each)
Obsidian or another immovable block to stop it
editionNote: Flying machines work in Java and Bedrock, but timing differs: in Java a moved observer pulses after its normal delay, while in Bedrock a moved observer always fires immediately. Many Java designs stall or run away on Bedrock, so copy a build tagged for your edition.
versions: Flying machines became possible when observers reached Java 1.11 (2016) - Pocket Edition had observers from 0.15.0. The 1.15 change that made slime and honey stop sticking to each other unlocked the modern two-part designs.

faq.q: Why does my flying machine not move?
faq.a: Count the blocks a single piston has to move - over 12 and it gives up silently. The other classic cause is an observer facing the wrong way: the dot (output) must point into the piston you want to trigger, and the face must watch the block that moves.

faq.q: How do I stop a flying machine?
faq.a: Put a block pistons cannot move in its path - obsidian, bedrock, a furnace or a chest all work. The engine bumps into it, the push fails and the loop dies. Some designs park on a leaf or glazed terracotta block instead.

faq.q: Can a flying machine go up or down?
faq.a: Yes, with a vertical layout - observers pointing up or down with pistons and slime arranged so the push-pull cycle climbs or descends. Vertical engines are fussier about block count, so start with a proven design block-for-block.

name: How to Make a Sugar Cane Farm in Minecraft
quickAnswer: Plant sugar cane on dirt or sand next to water and it grows one block every 18 minutes on average, up to 3 tall. An automatic farm watches the cane with observers and knocks the top off with pistons into hoppers or a water stream - zero replanting, endless paper for rockets, books and trading.
steps: Find starter cane. Sugar cane generates on riverbanks and shores in most biomes; the wandering trader also sells it. You only need one piece - it multiplies fast.
Plant it right. Cane goes on grass, dirt, sand or red sand directly adjacent to a water block (diagonals do not count). It needs no light and no farmland - water next door is the whole requirement.

Use the compact grid. A checkerboard of water sources with cane between them fits 4 canes per water block. Cover the water with lily pads or waterlogged slabs so you can walk the field without falling in.

Know the growth math. Every 16 random ticks the cane grows one block, which averages out to about one block per 18 minutes, stopping at 3 blocks naturally. Growth needs the chunk loaded, so build near your base or AFK spot.
Harvest the middle, keep the root. Break the middle block and the top falls too while the base replants itself - never break the bottom block or you replant by hand.

Automate with observer and piston. An observer watching the top growth level fires when cane reaches height 3, powering a piston that breaks the middle block. Drops fall into hoppers or a water stream to your chest.

Scale in layers. Stack identical rows with a 4-block gap between them, or run one long line of observers and pistons along a canal. A 20-plant starter farm already out-produces a manual field of any size.

Lily pads or slabs to cover the water

name: How to Make a Creeper Farm in Minecraft
quickAnswer: A creeper farm spawns creepers in a dark room with a trapdoor ceiling - exactly short enough that zombies and skeletons cannot spawn but creepers can - then flushes them with water to a kill zone. Even a small one produces around 700 gunpowder per hour, enough for all the TNT and firework rockets you will ever need.
steps: Pick the spot. Over an ocean is ideal: fewer caves below means almost every spawn happens inside your farm. On land, light up or slab every cave in range first, or rates collapse.
Build a dark spawning platform. Any solid blocks, completely dark inside, with a 2-block-high interior. Start with one layer about 8x8 and expand later - layers stack with 3 blocks of vertical space.

Add the trapdoor ceiling. Cover the ceiling with trapdoors so the effective height drops to 1 and 13/16 blocks. Creepers spawn in that space; zombies, skeletons and witches cannot. This trick is the whole farm.
Block the spiders. Spiders still fit under trapdoors. Place carpets on the floor with 2 empty blocks between them so no flat 3x3 area remains - spiders need that space and creepers do not.
Flush them out. Water streams push creepers to a central drop. To move them faster, place cats at the far end - creepers flee from cats and run straight into your water channel.
Kill for gunpowder. Campfires under the drop kill automatically and safely. For much better rates, drop them to half a heart and finish them with a Looting III sword.

AFK in the right place. Stand about 120 blocks above the farm on a platform so mobs spawn inside the farm but outside your 24-block no-spawn bubble. Check rates after 10 minutes and add layers if you want more.
materials: Stacks of solid building blocks and trapdoors
Cats (tame ocelots... cats - in a village or swamp hut)
Campfires or a Looting III sword
editionNote: The trapdoor height trick is Java-only: in Bedrock, creepers do not spawn under a 2-block trapdoor ceiling the same way, so Bedrock farms use other creeper-only layouts or accept mixed mobs with cat-scaring. Cat fleeing and campfire killing work on both.
versions: Creeper farms grew up with the trapdoor ceiling trick in the early versions, and boat/minecart mob storage (1.16) later enabled charged-creeper factories for mob heads. The classic small design still yields roughly 700 gunpowder per hour today.

faq.q: Why is my creeper farm so slow?
faq.a: Unlit caves and the surface around the farm eat your mob cap. Light up or slab everything in a 128-block sphere, or move the farm high over an ocean. Also make sure you AFK 24+ blocks from the platforms - mobs never spawn closer than that to you.

faq.q: How do I get only creepers and no other mobs?
faq.a: The trapdoor ceiling handles zombies and skeletons (Java), carpets spaced 2 apart handle spiders, and endermen cannot fit in a 2-high space anyway. What remains is creepers only.

faq.q: Campfires or Looting III?

name: How to Make a Gold Farm in Minecraft
quickAnswer: A gold farm mass-produces zombified piglins and funnels them to a kill zone for nuggets, ingots and XP. The simple version uses Nether portals (piglins spawn inside portal frames and step out into a trap); the fast version stacks spawn platforms on the Nether roof. Add turtle eggs to lure them and a Looting III sword to multiply the drops.
steps: Understand the two spawn sources. Zombified piglins spawn naturally in nether wastes (best rates), crimson forests and fortresses - and they also appear inside Nether portal blocks anywhere, because portals sit at exactly light level 11, the maximum they tolerate.

Start with the portal farm. In the Overworld or under the Nether bedrock ceiling, build large portal frames (up to 23x23 inside). Piglins spawn in the frame, wander out or get pushed by water, and fall to your kill zone. Cheap, safe and works from day one.

Lure with turtle eggs. Zombified piglins pathfind toward turtle eggs to crush them. An egg behind a pit or inside the portal area drags every spawned piglin exactly where you want it - no redstone needed.

Kill with Looting III. Manual kills with a Looting III sword multiply gold several times over and award XP when the piglins are angry at you. Hit one and the whole group aggros - shared anger is what makes XP modes work.

Scale to the Nether roof. Above the bedrock ceiling at Y 128+, build magma-block platforms (piglins spawn on magma, most mobs cannot) with an egg in the middle and drop chutes to a killing chamber. This is where the famous high-rate designs live.
Collect everything. Hoppers under the kill zone feed chests; add a simple sorter later so nuggets auto-craft into ingots and rotten flesh gets its own chest.

Know the rates. A basic portal farm is slow but free; mid designs reach dozens of gold blocks per hour; top Java roof designs quote 130-600 gold blocks per hour with Looting III - pick the size your patience allows.
materials: Obsidian for portal frames + flint and steel
Turtle eggs (from breeding turtles on beaches)
Magma blocks for roof platforms (optional, big farms)
Looting III sword, hoppers and chests
editionNote: Edition choice matters here. Natural-spawning roof farms are best on Java; on Bedrock, portal-based farms win because rapidly flickering portals spawn piglins much faster than natural spawning. Many famous Java designs simply do not work on Bedrock - copy one tagged for your edition.
versions: Zombified piglins replaced zombie pigmen in the 1.16 Nether Update, keeping the same farm mechanics. One recent caveat: Java 1.21.5 changed anger-based XP drops, so XP rates quoted for older designs may no longer apply - gold rates are unaffected.

faq.q: Why are no piglins spawning in my portal?
faq.a: Portal spawning is random-tick based and slow for small frames - a single 4x5 portal produces a trickle. Go bigger (23x23), stack several frames, and on Java make sure you are not in peaceful difficulty. Standing too close also blocks spawns: keep 24+ blocks away.

faq.q: Gold farm or bastion raiding?
faq.a: Raiding bastions is faster gold per minute early on, but finite and dangerous. A farm is infinite, safe once built, and doubles as an XP source. Most players raid one bastion for the fun, then build a farm for the supply.

faq.q: Do zombified piglins drop XP when killed automatically?
faq.a: XP comes from angered piglins dying, and Java 1.21.5 patched the always-drop-XP behavior for angered piglins, so pure fall-damage or cramming modes no longer guarantee XP. Manual Looting III kills remain the reliable XP method; automatic modes are now mainly for gold.

name: How to Make an XP Farm in Minecraft
quickAnswer: The fastest XP farm is an enderman farm in the End: drop endermen to one hit and finish them by hand for level 30 in under a minute. Before you reach the End, the best options are a monster spawner trap, a gold farm, or a furnace XP bank that stores smelting experience and pays it out all at once.
steps: Match the farm to your stage. Early game: spawner traps and quartz mining. Mid game: gold farms and furnace banks. Late game: the enderman farm beats everything by an order of magnitude.

Build a spawner trap first. Find a zombie or skeleton spawner in a dungeon, dig out a 9x9 room, and use water to push mobs to a drop that leaves them at one hit. About 24 minutes of grinding reaches level 30, plus enchanted drops you can disenchant at a grindstone for bonus XP.

Try the AFK skeleton trick. Tamed wolves attack skeletons without you swinging, so a skeleton spawner plus a pack of wolves farms XP while you are away - an 8-hour AFK session gives roughly 100 levels. Keep meat handy to heal the wolves.

Bank XP in your furnaces. Every item smelted stores a little experience inside the furnace. Feed it automatic fuel and items (a kelp or cactus farm), let it run for days, then pull one item out by hand and collect all the stored XP at once.
Upgrade to a gold farm. Angered zombified piglins killed by hand give steady XP plus gold - a mid-size design takes you to level 130+ in about 30 minutes with a Looting III sword.

Finish with the enderman farm. On the main End island, bridge 200 blocks away from the island, build a spawning platform at Y 1 with an endermite lure, and drop endermen 43 blocks to a killing pad. Sweep a sword through their feet: level 30 in under a minute, the fastest XP in the game.
Spend it wisely. Enchant at 30, repair Mending gear as you go, and never carry more levels than you can afford to lose - death still takes almost everything.
materials: Early: water buckets, building blocks, torches (spawner trap)
Wolves + bones for the AFK skeleton version
Furnaces + kelp or cactus for an XP bank
Late: ender pearls, an endermite in a minecart, leaf blocks
editionNote: All of these work in Java and Bedrock, but rates differ: enderman farm rates depend on simulation distance and spawning rules that favor Java designs, and Bedrock spawner traps often need different water layouts. Copy a build tagged for your edition and version.
versions: XP farms have evolved with the game: spawner traps are as old as dungeons, gold farms moved to the Nether roof in 1.16, and 1.21.5 trimmed anger-based piglin XP. The enderman farm has been the speed king since the End opened in 1.0.

faq.q: What is the fastest XP farm in Minecraft?
faq.a: The enderman farm in the End - level 30 in under a minute once it is built. For pre-End worlds, a gold farm is the fastest practical option, and a skeleton spawner with tamed wolves is the best fully AFK one.

faq.q: Why do I lose all my XP when I die?
faq.a: Dying drops your experience where you fell and you only recover part of it, capped at around level 7 worth. Bank levels into enchantments and repairs as you earn them, and use an ender chest for valuables before risky trips.

faq.q: Mob farm or spawner farm for XP?
faq.a: A general mob farm gives better loot variety but mediocre XP per hour. A spawner trap is concentrated and faster for pure levels. If you want both, build the mob farm first for gunpowder and strings, then a dedicated XP source.

name: How to Make a Raid Farm in Minecraft
quickAnswer: A raid farm triggers raids against a controlled "village" - often a single villager with a bed and a job block - and funnels every wave into a kill zone. It prints emeralds and totems of undying, and on Bedrock also enchanted books and iron gear. The basic version takes an afternoon and supplies totems for the rest of the game.
steps: Get the omen. Since 1.21, kill a raid captain (pillager outposts spawn them) to get an ominous bottle, drink it for raid omen, and walk into your farm village - the raid starts. Before 1.21 the captain gave Bad Omen directly, which is why old guides look different.

Build the fake village. One villager linked to a bed (plus a job block for safety) defines the raid center. Keep it small and far from real villages - anything else with beds or villagers can hijack the raid center.

Choose the spawn trap. Raiders spawn near the raid center. Wall off the area so the only valid spawn is a water funnel platform above your killing chamber; on Bedrock build the platform over an ocean because raiders will not pathfind toward the villager.

Set up the kill zone. Drop raiders far enough to leave them at one hit, then finish them by hand for the loot and XP. A lava blade or magma layer handles ravagers, which are too big for standard drops.
Survive the waves. A raid comes in waves (3 on easy, 5 on normal, 7 on hard). Evokers summon vexes that fly through walls - kill evokers first and keep your totem in the off-hand.
Collect the loot. Emeralds, totems of undying, saddles and enchanted gear flow into hoppers. Totems do not stack, so late-game designs use allays to sort them into bulk storage.

Chain the next raid. When the raid ends you get Hero of the Village (cheaper trades - nice bonus). Drink another ominous bottle and go again; expect a roughly 30-second reset between raids on current versions.
materials: Building blocks, water buckets, signs or trapdoors for the funnel
Lava or magma blocks for ravagers
Hoppers and chests; allays for totem sorting (optional)
editionNote: Java and Bedrock raid farms are completely different builds. Java raiders sprint toward the village center, so bed-bait funnels work; Bedrock raiders do not, so spawns must be forced onto an ocean platform - but Bedrock raids also drop emeralds, enchanted books and iron gear, making those farms especially rich.
versions: Raid farms date to the 1.14 Village & Pillage update that introduced raids. The 1.21 ominous bottle change (raid omen instead of instant Bad Omen) slowed the top farms but they remain the best totem and emerald source in the game.

faq.q: Is a raid farm worth it?
faq.a: Yes - it is the only renewable totem of undying source, and the emeralds make villager prices irrelevant. Even the basic one-afternoon design produces enough totems for the rest of a playthrough.

faq.q: Why did my raid spawn outside the trap?
faq.a: The raid center moved or there are valid spawn spaces you missed. Confirm your villager is still linked to the bed inside the farm, remove stray beds and villagers within about 96 blocks, and spawn-proof every surface near the platform.

faq.q: Raid farm or villager trading for emeralds?
faq.a: Trading is steady and safe from day one; a raid farm is bursty and far richer once built, and it is the only source that also gives totems. Most players trade early, then build the farm and never worry about emeralds again.

name: How to Make a Bamboo Farm in Minecraft
quickAnswer: Plant bamboo on almost any dirt-like block - no water needed - and it rockets up: about one block per 68 seconds on Java, up to 12-16 blocks tall. An observer watching the growth fires pistons that mow the field into hoppers, giving you unlimited scaffolding, sticks, fuel and wood-tier blocks.
steps: Get starter bamboo. Fish it up in jungles, loot it from jungle temples and shipwreck supply chests, or break wild bamboo in jungle biomes. One shoot is enough.

Plant it anywhere dry. Bamboo grows on grass, dirt, coarse dirt, gravel, mycelium, podzol, moss, sand, red sand and mud - no water, no farmland. Leave light level 9 or above at the top of the plants or growth stalls.

Know the speed. On Java (random tick speed 3) each plant grows roughly every 68 seconds; on Bedrock (speed 1) it is about every 205 seconds. Bone meal adds 1-2 blocks instantly. Bamboo tops out at 12-16 blocks.
Harvest like sugar cane. Break any block and everything above falls - cut at the second block and the base regrows. A sword sweeps bamboo fastest.

Automate the small version. Plant a double row of 8 on mud (16 plants), face two rows of pistons inward at second-block height, and hang an observer 5 blocks above the plants. When bamboo reaches it, both piston rows fire and drops land in hopper minecarts or hoppers below.

Scale with a flying machine. For bulk fuel or scaffolding, a two-way flying machine sweeps a whole field on each pass: observers trigger it, hoppers underneath collect. Keep the field bounded or the harvest can flood your world with entities.
Feed the furnace. Bamboo smelts only 0.25 items per piece, but a farm produces thousands - route the output straight into your furnace array and it burns forever, the classic infinite fuel loop.
materials: Per auto-module: pistons, observers, hoppers or hopper minecarts
Torches or lanterns (light 9+ at the top)
editionNote: Same design works in both editions, but Bedrock grows bamboo at one third of Java speed (default random tick speed 1 vs 3), so Bedrock farms need roughly three times the planted area for the same output. Bone meal works on bamboo in both editions.
versions: Bamboo arrived in Java 1.14 (Village & Pillage, 18w43a) and Bedrock 1.8.0. The 1.20 bamboo wood set (planks, mosaic, rafts) turned it from a scaffolding crop into a full wood alternative, which is when farms really took off.

faq.q: Why is my bamboo not growing?
faq.a: Two checks: the top of the plant needs light level 9+, and the chunk must be loaded. If both are fine, it is just Bedrock pace - three times slower than Java. Bone meal confirms the plant is healthy: it should add 1-2 blocks instantly.

faq.q: Bamboo or kelp for furnace fuel?
faq.a: Kelp smelts into dried kelp blocks (20 items each) and is denser per craft, but needs water and an extra smelting step. Bamboo burns raw with zero crafting and the farm is simpler and lag-friendlier. For huge furnace arrays most players run bamboo.

faq.q: How big should my bamboo farm be?
faq.a: A 16-plant piston module keeps one furnace array fed and covers personal scaffolding needs. For super-smelters or bulk bamboo wood, go to a flying-machine field - a few hundred plants produces more than any chest system wants.

name: How to Make a Villager Trading Hall in Minecraft
quickAnswer: A trading hall lines up villagers in individual cells, each with its job site block, so you can trade with dozens of professionals in one room. The three parts are: input (a breeder feeding new villagers in), storage (safe cells with workstations), and output (a way to discard bad traders without tanking your reputation).
steps: Start with a villager breeder. A hall needs a steady supply of fresh villagers, and kidnapping them from villages one by one gets old fast. Build the breeder first, next to the hall site.

Plan the three parts. Input: a rail or water channel that delivers new villagers into empty cells and closes behind them. Storage: one cell per villager with its job site block in reach. Output: a disposal route for rejects.

Build the cells. One-block-wide cells with a work station at the back and a slab or trapdoor at the front keep villagers in place and let you reach the trade button. Tile them in rows with a walkway in front.

Assign professions by placement. An unemployed villager claims the nearest unclaimed job site block, so place the workstation you want (lectern for librarian, blast furnace for armorer...) right at the cell before the villager arrives.

Reroll before you trade. Never trade with a villager until it offers what you want: break and replace its job block to reroll the novice trades as many times as you like. The first trade locks the profession and offers forever.

Protect the hall. Light it up, wall it off and keep zombies out - one zombie inside converts your whole hall. Lightning turns villagers into witches, so add a roof. Workstations within reach let them restock twice a day.

Discard without reputation damage. Never kill villagers by hand: it drops your reputation, raises prices and can turn iron golems hostile. Route rejects with water or rails to lava or fire, which does not credit you with the kill - or better, recycle them into an iron farm or crop farm.

Zombify and cure for discounts. Advanced halls add a zombie chamber: let a zombie convert a villager, cure it, and that villager gives you permanent major discounts. On Hard difficulty conversion is guaranteed.
materials: Villager breeder next door (beds + food + 2 starter villagers)
Job site blocks: lecterns, blast furnaces, composters...
Rails and minecarts or water channels for transport
Building blocks, slabs, lighting and a roof
Lava or fire for the disposal system
editionNote: The hall concept is identical in Java and Bedrock. Details differ: Bedrock villagers must be linked to a bed to restock trades, and each level unlocks up to three trade slots instead of two - so Bedrock halls include beds, while Java halls can skip them. Automatic zombification modules exist for both.
versions: Trading halls became practical with the 1.14 Village & Pillage update, which tied professions to job site blocks and made trades rerollable until the first trade. The mechanics have been stable since, with the experimental Villager Trade Rebalance still optional.

faq.q: How do I reroll a villager's trades?
faq.a: Break its job site block and place it back - as long as you have never traded with that villager, it loses and reclaims the profession with fresh offers. Once you trade even once, the trades are locked forever, so reroll first, trade after.

faq.q: Why did my villager lose its profession?
faq.a: It lost access to its claimed job site block - broken, moved or blocked. If it has never traded, it simply becomes unemployed and can claim a new station. A traded villager keeps its profession even without a station, but cannot restock.

faq.q: Is killing bad traders bad for me?
faq.a: Yes if you do it by hand: player kills hurt your village reputation, which raises prices and eventually turns iron golems hostile. Lava, fire or fall damage do not count against you - or skip killing entirely and move rejects to an iron farm.

name: How to Make a Villager Breeder in Minecraft
quickAnswer: Villagers breed on their own when three things line up: spare beds (more beds than villagers), enough food in their pockets (12 food points: 3 bread, or 12 carrots, potatoes or beetroots each), and 2 full blocks of air above every bed. Build a small room with beds and two villagers, toss food at them, and babies follow.
steps: Isolate the site. Villagers detect villages in an 80-block sphere - build the breeder at least that far from any real village, iron farm or trading hall so bed counting does not get confused.
Bring two villagers. Boat them over land or rail them with minecarts. Any two adults work; a farmer as one of them makes the breeder self-feeding later.

Place the beds. At least 3 valid beds (one per adult plus spare for babies). Each bed needs 2 full blocks of free space above it - slabs and trapdoors over a bed invalidate it, because the baby must be able to bounce on the bed.

Feed them. Throw food at their feet: villagers need 12 food points to become willing. Bread is worth 4 points (3 loaves per villager), carrots, potatoes and beetroots 1 point each (12 per villager). They pick it up into their hidden inventory.

Wait for hearts. When both are willing and the bed census shows spare capacity, heart particles appear and a baby villager pops out. The census runs about once a minute - no hearts usually means a bed problem.

Automate with a farmer. Give one villager a composter and a crop plot: farmer villagers harvest and throw surplus food at the others, so the breeder runs forever with zero feeding. A wheat or carrot plot next to the beds is the classic layout.
Export the babies. Babies cannot claim beds until they grow (20 minutes), so drop them through a trapdoor shaft onto rails or a water stream straight to your trading hall cells.
Scale carefully. More spare beds means more babies, but the adults only share food so fast. Two adults plus 6-8 beds and a farmer already out-produces any hall you will build.
materials: 3-8 beds with 2 blocks of air above each
Bread, carrots, potatoes or beetroots (12 points per villager)
Composter + crop plot for the self-feeding version
Rails or water channels for baby export
editionNote: Core mechanics are the same in Java and Bedrock: beds, food points and the 80-block village radius. The 2-blocks-above-the-bed requirement is long-standing; verify unusual ceiling blocks on your edition, and remember Bedrock villagers also need bed links to restock trades later in the hall.
versions: The bed-and-food breeding system arrived with 1.14 Village & Pillage, replacing the old door-counting rule where villagers bred based on "valid doors". The 12 food points and spare-bed census have been unchanged since.

faq.q: Why are my villagers not breeding?
faq.a: Check in order: spare beds (more beds than villagers), 2 blocks of air above every bed, food thrown at their feet (they must pick it up), and no other village within 80 blocks stealing the bed count. No hearts after a minute almost always means one of those four.

faq.q: How much food do villagers need to breed?
faq.a: 12 food points each. Bread counts 4 (3 loaves), carrots, potatoes and beetroots count 1 (12 items). Mix and match - a villager holding 2 bread and 4 carrots is willing too.

faq.q: Can villagers breed forever on their own?
faq.a: Only until the beds fill up: the population census stops willingness once villagers equal or exceed valid beds. Keep exporting the babies to your hall and the breeder keeps producing. A farmer villager handles the food side indefinitely.

name: How to Cure a Zombie Villager in Minecraft
quickAnswer: Hit a zombie villager with a splash potion of Weakness, then right-click it with a regular golden apple (not enchanted). It shudders, gains Strength, and turns back into a villager after 3-5 minutes. Cured villagers give you permanent trading discounts - this is how players get one-emerald trades.
steps: Find a zombie villager. 5% of natural zombie spawns are zombie villagers (in Bedrock they appear in groups of 2-4), and any zombie that kills a villager can convert it - 100% on Hard, 50% on Normal, 0% on Easy.
Trap it safely. Lure it into a boat, minecart or a small dark cell before starting. Curing takes minutes and the mob keeps attacking you the whole time - plus it burns in daylight like any zombie.
Brew Weakness. A splash potion of Weakness needs only a fermented spider eye brewed into a water bottle (gunpowder to make it splash) - no Nether wart required, so it works from day one.
Craft a golden apple. 8 gold ingots around a regular apple. The enchanted golden apple does NOT work for curing - it must be the plain one.
Apply both. Splash the Weakness (gray particles), then use the golden apple on it. It starts shuddering and gains Strength - it hits HARDER while curing, so keep your distance or keep it boxed in.
Wait 3-5 minutes. The cure timer is 3 to 5 minutes at random. Surrounding it with iron bars and beds (within a 9x9x9 cube) speeds it up slightly - about 4% faster with 14 or more.
Collect your villager. It transforms with a brief Nausea effect. If it had a profession before zombification, it keeps it; if it had ever traded, it keeps its exact trades too.
Trade at a discount. Your cured villager gives you permanent major discounts; nearby villagers give smaller ones. Re-curing the same villager does not stack further discounts - one cure each.
materials: Splash potion of Weakness (fermented spider eye + water bottle + gunpowder)
Golden apple (8 gold ingots + 1 apple) - NOT the enchanted one
Boat, minecart or a secure cell
Optional: iron bars and beds to speed up the cure
editionNote: Curing works the same in Java and Bedrock, with small differences: Bedrock cured nitwits become employable (Java nitwits stay nitwits), and in Bedrock nearby villagers within 16 blocks also give small discounts scaling with up to 10 cured villagers. Both editions grant the permanent personal discount.
versions: Curing has existed since zombie villagers arrived in 1.4.2 (2012), with the Weakness-plus-golden-apple recipe unchanged since. The iron bars and bed speed boost is an intentional nod to the classic "zombie doctor" setup, and the permanent discount system arrived with 1.14's gossip mechanics.

faq.q: Why is the golden apple not working on the zombie villager?
faq.a: Two usual causes: it is the enchanted (Notch) apple - only the plain golden apple cures - or the zombie villager does not have the Weakness effect active. Splash Weakness first, watch for the gray swirl particles, then use the apple.

faq.q: Does curing give discounts in both editions?
faq.a: Yes. The curing player gets a permanent major discount in Java and Bedrock. Bedrock additionally spreads small discounts to nearby villagers (scaling up to 10 cured villagers), while Java shares reputation through gossip. Re-curing the same villager adds nothing.

faq.q: How do I get a zombie villager to convert my librarian?
faq.a: Trap the librarian with the zombie in a confined space on Hard difficulty - conversion is guaranteed there (50% on Normal, never on Easy). Then cure the result. This "zombify and cure" loop is the standard way to discount an entire trading hall.
